notes: Jatavarman Sundara Pandya (c.1258) defeated Rajendra III and imposed vassalage. Kaveri delta then held under the Pandya emperor, and no Chola records survive after 1279. Hoysala and Kadava interventions came before. Polonnaruwa and Kampili did not hold the core.

source2: M. A. Fitzgerald, The Rulers of Larsa (PhD diss., Yale University, 2002), p. 25 - https://uruk-warka.dk/news/2023/THE_RULERS_OF_LARSA.pdf
notes: Hammurabi of Babylon defeated Rim-Sin, took Larsa (1763 BC; Fitzgerald gives 1762) and replaced Larsa's authority with his own. Rim-Sin's earlier wars against Isin, Uruk and Babylon coalitions are coded as inter-state wars, not internal crisis.

source1: Karen Radner, 'Israel, the House of Omri', Assyrian Empire Builders, University College London, 2012 - https://www.ucl.ac.uk/sargon/essentials/countries/israel/
notes: Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria three years. It fell in 722 (Sargon II claimed it; some date it 720) and became an Assyrian province. Coups followed Jeroboam II; Galilee was lost in 732. Listed capital Jerusalem reflects the United Monarchy.

source1: Peter C. Perdue, China Marches West: The Qing Conquest of Central Eurasia, Harvard University Press (Belknap), 2005/2010 - https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674057432
notes: Galdan Tseren's death (1745) set off succession wars (Lama Dorji, Dawachi, Amursana). A Qing army took Ili in 1755 and captured Dawachi; Amursana's revolt was crushed by 1757. The core was the Ili valley (Ghulja), not the Orkhon as listed.

source1: Krishnendu Ray, 'Khadga Dynasty', Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh) - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Khadga_Dynasty
notes: Banglapedia dates the Khadgas in Vanga/Samatata to c.625-705 (database: 650-700). How their rule ended is not documented. The Devas 'might have supplanted' them in the 8th century. Only one scholarly source could be opened.

successor: Adal Sultanate (continuing; later Imamate of Aussa)
notes: 1543 is Ahmad Gragn's death, not the polity's end. Adal continued from Harar until Ethiopian and Oromo pressure moved the capital to Aussa in 1577. Ajuran is not a successor. The 1520s Abu Bakr-Ahmad conflict counts as internal crisis.

successor: Kingdom of Hungary under the Anjou dynasty
notes: Andrew III's death (1301) ended the Árpád line. The kingdom continued under Charles Robert of Anjou (crowned 1301, recognised 1308, crowned again 1310) after a contest with Wenceslas and Otto. Late-13th-century baronial fragmentation counts as internal crisis.

Chandragupta ended Nanda rule c.321 BC. Classical sources suggest he raised his army in the northwest, outside the Nanda realm, so coded T2. His campaign order and insider status are disputed. Only one source could be opened.

source1: none opened (web-fetch budget exhausted; Wikipedia used for leads only)
notes: Subject tribes (Basmyl, Uyghur, Karluk) revolted in 742 and killed Ozmish in 744. The Uyghurs killed the last khagan in 745 and founded their khaganate at Ötüken. A vassal revolt is internal, so T1c. Succession turmoil followed Bilge's death (734).

Khasekhemwy ended the mid-2nd-dynasty internal struggles (their extent is debated). His queen was probably mother of the first 3rd-dynasty kings; Djoser was related through his mother. A dynastic change within one state. Britannica dates run lower (2nd dynasty c.2730-2590).
